newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia, a year after Dayton, 'not so bad' - Bildt.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia, a year after Dayton, 'not so bad' - Bildt.

text.p: One year after Bosnia's peace accord was signed, the international community's coordinator Carl Bildt gave an upbeat asessment of the accord's achievements on Thursday but said a lot more needs to be done.

"Things have been done, things are moving, but at the same time most of agenda remains to be fulfilled and that is why we are here and why there will be another working day tomorrow," Bildt told reporters in Sarajevo.

The U.S.-sponsored negotiations in Dayton, Ohio last year produced an accord that silenced Bosnia's guns but also promised to stitch the torn country together and reverse the politics of ethnic purity that nationalists had fought for.
While the military parts of the accord managed to tuck former enemy armies into barracks overseen by NATO, critics say the agreement achieved little of the civilian aspects.
They say Dayton could fall well short of achieving its key objectives of locking up war criminals, restoring freedom of movement across front lines and returning refugees to their homes.
Only seven of 75 war crimes suspects are in custody, freedom of movement is confined to one's own ethnic area, and barely a trickle of refugees are going home.

"If there was anyone who thought that everything (in the Dayton Accord) would be realised in one year, that person was rather naive, but a foundation had been laid and in comparison with what was the situation a year ago...it's not that bad," Bildt said.
Insisting there is no such thing as an instant peace, Bildt called upon Bosnia's three national leaders to step up the pace in setting up joint bodies.
"Common institutions -- they are the key to what's going to happen in the years to come," he said.
But Moslem, Croat and Serb leaders have so far failed to agree on a joint government and Serb deputies snubbed the inaugural session of the national parliament, effectively blocking its work.
Bildt warned that a lack of joint institutions could have a serious impact on a donors information conference in Brussels on December 2-3 and another fund-pledging conference set for next year.
"You can hardly have a donors information conference if there are no common institutions of Bosnia to be there and present their case," he said.
"The longer they are delayed in setting up, the more we risk delays in the vital economic and social progress."
